units.t: Myths & Religions Shorts.
In this episode: Día de Muertos: a festival for the dead and King Arthur: how a legend was built.
Part one. Día de Muertos: a festival for the dead.
Each year at the start of November, families across Mexico build glowing altars and lay paths of orange petals so that their dead can find the way home.
It is a celebration, not a horror show.
Not Mexican Halloween.
Día de Muertos, the Day of the Dead, is often lumped in with Halloween because the dates are close and both involve skulls.
The spirit is very different.
Halloween plays with fear; Día de Muertos is about love and remembrance.
Families believe their departed relatives return for a short visit, and the living prepare to welcome them as honoured guests.
The main days are 1 and 2 November.
In many places the first day honours children who have died, sometimes called los angelitos, the little angels, and the second honours adults.
Customs vary greatly from region to region, and Indigenous communities often keep some of the most distinctive traditions.
Two worlds meet.
Long before the Spanish arrived, peoples of Mesoamerica, including the Aztecs, held ceremonies honouring the dead.
Death was seen as part of a cycle rather than a final end, and the Aztec underworld, Mictlan, was ruled by Mictlantecuhtli and his consort Mictecacihuatl.
After the Spanish conquest in the sixteenth century, missionaries promoted the Catholic feasts of All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day on 1 and 2 November.
Over centuries, local practices and Catholic customs wove together.
Historians debate how much of today's festival comes directly from pre-Hispanic religion, since some features developed much later.
What is clear is that the result is uniquely Mexican, neither simply Indigenous nor simply European.
The ofrenda.
The heart of the celebration is the ofrenda, an altar built in homes, and sometimes in schools, offices and public squares.
It usually has several tiers covered in cloth and decorated with papel picado, delicate tissue paper cut into patterns.
Photographs of the dead take pride of place, along with things they loved in life: a favourite dish, a bottle of tequila, cigarettes, sweets, toys for children.
Candles light the way, and copal incense perfumes the air.
Many families include water to quench the souls' thirst after their long journey, and salt for purification.
Building the ofrenda is a family task, and telling stories about the people pictured is part of the point.
Remembering keeps the dead present.
Marigolds and sugar skulls.
The flower of the season is the cempasúchil, a vivid orange marigold whose name comes from the Nahuatl language.
Its strong colour and scent are believed to guide souls, and families scatter petals in paths from the street, or the cemetery, to the altar.
Bakeries fill with pan de muerto, a soft, sweet bread often flavoured with orange blossom and decorated with strips of dough shaped like bones.
Sugar skulls, calaveras de azúcar, are moulded from sugar and decorated with coloured icing, sometimes with a person's name across the forehead.
They are cheerful and bright rather than morbid.
They express a familiar attitude: death comes to everyone, so it may as well be met with a smile.
Cemetery, Catrina and heritage.
In many towns, families clean and decorate graves with marigolds, candles and offerings, and some keep vigil through the night.
On Janitzio island in Lake Pátzcuaro, Purépecha fishermen cross the lake in canoes carrying lights.
The mood is warm and social, closer to a family reunion than a funeral.
Skeletons dressed as living people have long mocked the powerful in Mexico.
In the early 1910s, printmaker José Guadalupe Posada etched a skeleton woman in a grand feathered hat, mocking Mexicans who imitated European fashion.
Diego Rivera placed her in his 1947 mural, and she became La Catrina.
UNESCO listed the festival in 2008.
The film Spectre, 2015, invented a Mexico City parade, which the city then staged for real, and Pixar's Coco, 2017, spread the ofrenda worldwide.
The key idea: Día de Muertos is a family celebration of love and remembrance, not a spooky festival.
Part two. King Arthur: how a legend was built.
There may never have been a King Arthur.
Yet over a thousand years, writers in Wales, England and France assembled Camelot, the Round Table and the Holy Grail piece by piece.
Faint traces after Rome.
Roman authority in Britain collapsed in the early fifth century.
Over the next two hundred years, Anglo-Saxon groups settled much of what became England, while Britons held out in the west and north.
Written records are extremely thin, which is why legends could flourish.
A British monk, Gildas, writing in the sixth century, described a British victory over the Saxons at Mount Badon.
Tellingly, he never mentions Arthur.
The earliest possible reference is in a Welsh poem, Y Gododdin, which praises a warrior as brave, "though he was no Arthur".
Its date is uncertain and the line may be a later addition.
From these faint traces, a towering figure would grow.
Twelve battles.
Around 830, the Latin Historia Brittonum, traditionally linked to a monk named Nennius, listed twelve battles fought by Arthur, a "leader of battles", ending at Badon.
Some sites are impossible to locate, and one passage has him carrying an image of the Virgin Mary into combat.
A later Welsh chronicle, the Annales Cambriae, records Badon and also Camlann, "in which Arthur and Medraut fell".
Medraut would become the treacherous Mordred.
Early Welsh poems and tales show a different Arthur, leading heroes against giants, witches and a monstrous boar.
Most historians now think there is not enough evidence to say whether a real Arthur existed, though the debate continues.
Geoffrey's bestseller.
The Arthur most people know was launched by Geoffrey of Monmouth, a cleric in Oxford.
His History of the Kings of Britain, completed around 1136, claimed to be translated from an ancient British book, a claim most scholars doubt.
Geoffrey gave Arthur a dramatic life.
Merlin's magic lets Uther Pendragon visit Igerna at Tintagel, and Arthur is conceived.
As king, Arthur defeats the Saxons, conquers much of Europe and challenges Rome itself.
While he is away, his nephew Mordred seizes the throne and Guinevere.
Arthur returns, kills Mordred and is mortally wounded, then carried to the island of Avalon to be healed.
The book was a medieval sensation, surviving in more than two hundred manuscripts.
Knights, table and Grail.
Writers across the Channel dressed Geoffrey's warrior king in courtly fashion.
In 1155 the Norman poet Wace retold the history in French verse and introduced the Round Table, where no knight could claim the place of honour.
Later, Chrétien de Troyes shifted attention from Arthur to his knights.
He gave us the earliest surviving story of Lancelot's love for Guinevere, and first mentioned Camelot.
Chrétien's unfinished Perceval, from the 1180s, introduced a mysterious graal, a serving dish carried in a procession.
He died before explaining it.
Soon Robert de Boron identified the Grail as the vessel of the Last Supper, and later romances made the quest a spiritual test that most knights failed.
The pure Galahad, Lancelot's son, achieves it.
Malory and the returning king.
In 1191, monks at Glastonbury Abbey announced they had found the grave of Arthur and Guinevere.
The abbey needed funds and pilgrims after a fire, and many historians suspect the find was staged.
It still tied Avalon to Glastonbury.
Nearly three centuries later, Sir Thomas Malory, who wrote at least part of his work in prison, gathered the French and English stories into one English prose narrative.
William Caxton printed it in 1485 as Le Morte d'Arthur, and it became the main source for later English retellings.
Legend said Arthur would return in Britain's hour of need, and he has.
Tennyson made him a model of Victorian duty.
T.
H.
White used him to think about power after two world wars.
Arthur stands for the hope of a just ruler, and the sadness when good kingdoms fall.
The key idea: Arthur's story grew from very thin records in the obscure centuries after Roman rule ended in Britain.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. How does Día de Muertos differ from Halloween?
Answer. It welcomes the dead home with love.
Question two. Why could Arthur legends flourish in the centuries after Rome?
Answer. Written records from the period are extremely thin.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
